documents.title: AI Syllabus Statements
documents.stance_why: The page offers sample syllabus statements at three levels (permissive, mixed-use, unpermitted) plus an optional required-AI addition, and says "Faculty can create customized AI policies for each course", so it sets no single stance and delegates to instructors via tiers.
tiers: Optional addition: AI required for some assignments
documents.summary: A university AI office page giving faculty template syllabus statements for student AI use, from permissive-with-disclosure to unpermitted, plus an optional required-AI clause. It also sets a FERPA-based student data protection statement that binds faculty use of AI.

units.why: "Adding AI policies to courses helps set clear expectations for students and protects academic integrity" explains why syllabus AI statements are worthwhile; it is a rationale for syllabus communication (P09), not an order, so informs.
units.anchor: Adding AI policies to courses helps set clear expectations for students
units.frag_start: Adding AI policies to courses helps
units.fit_note: Framed as a benefit of syllabus statements rather than an explicit requirement. States the benefit of syllabus statements rather than a requirement to include one; no mandate is stated.
units.resolution_why: A coded should (benefit read as a nudge to add a statement); B coded informs. The source says only that adding AI policies "helps set clear expectations" and does not tell instructors to do so, so informs with neutral stance follows.

units.why: Warns that without guidelines students "may be confused" and commit "unintentional violations or missed learning opportunities"; explains the need for explicit expectations, so communication rationale (P09) rather than a stance.
units.anchor: Without clear guidelines, students may be confused about what AI use is acceptable
units.fit_note: Rationale for stating expectations, not the requirement itself. Rationale for clarity rather than a rule requiring a statement.

units.why: "Faculty are expected to abide by these restrictions on their own AI use, regardless of whether the statement is included in their syllabus" binds faculty to the data-protection limits; P50 protects student data.
units.anchor: Faculty are expected to abide by these restrictions on their own AI use

units.why: "explicit written consent, as required under FERPA" before faculty enter student data into a third-party AI tool: a data-protection rule for faculty, P50 (not P20, which concerns students).
units.anchor: unless you give explicit written consent, as required under FERPA

units.why: "data-minimization principle - only the smallest amount of information possible" limits what faculty share with AI tools; privacy rule, P50.
units.anchor: only the smallest amount of information possible will be used

units.why: 'Any vendor employed by the university must have FERPA-compliant data-protection policies' sets a vetting requirement on AI vendors; admin-level approval of tools and vendors, so P65 rather than P50 because the rule is about vendor eligibility.
units.anchor: Any vendor employed by the university must have
units.fit_note: Vendor requirement is about data-protection compliance, not contract review or data-sharing limits.

units.why: 'this must be transparent to you (e.g., privacy policy, encryption, data disposal)' requires vendors' safeguards to be visible to students; a transparency duty on data protection, nearest P50.
units.anchor: this must be transparent to you
units.fit_note: Transparency of vendor safeguards to students; P50 centers on protecting data and vetted tools. The rule is transparency of vendor safeguards to students, not the protection itself.
units.resolution_why: Found only by B: the same sentence as the vendor-compliance unit adds a second rule, "this must be transparent to you" (safeguards visible to students). Real policy statement, so kept as its own unit. Nearest type is P50 (data protection and vetted tools) since no type covers vendor transparency to students; P65 is about the review itself.

units.why: "You will be informed about what data (if any) is shared, provided, or stored when we use any AI tool in the classroom" commits instructors to tell students about their AI tool use; P47 (disclose instructor AI use).
units.anchor: You will be informed about what data (if any) is shared
units.fit_note: Disclosure concerns data shared with AI tools used in class, not only grading or feedback. Disclosure concerns data handling in instructor AI use, not grading or feedback methods.
units.resolution_why: Both coders gave P47, must, instructor, course-start; they differed on unit_stance (A permit, B restrict). The passage is a duty to tell students what data is shared when AI is used in class; it neither permits nor limits AI, so it is coded require, the stance used for disclosure duties.

units.why: 'and you can opt out' gives students the right to opt out of AI tool use involving their data in class; a choice guarantee, nearest P51 (AI optional, alternatives) though the opt-out is about data.
units.anchor: and you can opt out
units.frag_start: You will be informed about what
units.fit_note: Opt-out concerns instructor-chosen AI tools that process student data, not student AI use. Opt-out concerns student data in instructor-used AI tools, not cost or access to student AI tools.
units.resolution_why: A coded informs/neutral, B coded may/permit. "and you can opt out" gives students a right to opt out of AI tools used in class, so may is right; it does not change what AI is allowed, so unit_stance is neutral.

units.why: "Faculty can create customized AI policies for each course based on their teaching goals" leaves the decision to instructors; P04 is primary (P83, objectives, is secondary).
units.anchor: Faculty can create customized AI policies for each course
units.resolution_why: A coded neutral, B coded permit. "Faculty can create customized AI policies for each course" is a statement that the rule is set by the instructor (P04); it grants authority over course rules rather than permitting AI use, so neutral.

units.why: "AI-intensive courses may require detailed policies, while others might prohibit the use of AI entirely" notes the range from detailed policy to full prohibition; informs on variation, P04.
units.anchor: while others might prohibit the use of AI entirely

units.why: "Since AI violations can be hard to detect, requiring students to disclose AI usage may be more practical than outright bans" admits detection limits and prefers disclosure to bans; P82 fits best, disclosure preference noted.
units.anchor: Since AI violations can be hard to detect
units.fit_note: Also recommends disclosure requirements over bans (P24). Also advises disclosure over bans as the practical response; that part is close to P24.
units.resolution_why: A coded should/permit, B informs/neutral. The sentence says violations "can be hard to detect" (the P82 fact) and adds that requiring disclosure "may be more practical than outright bans". The main assertion is the acknowledgement; the advice is hedged ("may be"), so informs/neutral. Both fit notes kept because the disclosure advice is not captured by P82.

units.why: Heading "Permissive & Reflective Policy (AI encouraged with disclosure)" with the mixed-use and unpermitted samples names categories of AI policy; P05 names tiers.
units.anchor: Permissive & Reflective Policy (AI encouraged with disclosure)
units.fit_note: Three sample statements: permissive, mixed-use, unpermitted.
units.resolution_why: Found only by A: the heading names the sample tiers (permissive, mixed-use, unpermitted), which is the tier structure of P05. Real statement of the document's structure, kept.

units.why: The permissive sample says 'You are invited to use AI tools strategically in this course'; AI is welcomed by default with disclosure, so P02, encourage.
units.anchor: You are invited to use AI tools strategically in this course
units.frag_start: You are invited to use AI tools

units.why: "to brainstorm, draft, analyze, or revise" lists permitted uses; brainstorming is the specific permission, P15, though drafting and revising go wider.
units.anchor: to brainstorm, draft, analyze, or revise
units.fit_note: Also permits drafting, analyzing and revising, not only brainstorming. Also lists drafting, analyzing and revising, which span P91 and P89.

units.why: "briefly explain how you used the tool" in a note or method section requires disclosure with the submission, naming tool and use; P24.
units.anchor: briefly explain how you used the tool

units.why: 'If you choose not to use AI in your learning process, that is perfectly acceptable' makes AI optional with no penalty; P51 (AI not required).
units.anchor: If you choose not to use AI in your learning process, that is perfectly acceptable
units.frag_start: If you choose not to use AI
units.fit_note: Frames choosing not to use AI as acceptable rather than addressing cost or accommodations.
units.resolution_why: A anchored a shorter span, B the fuller sentence; same rule. Kept B's anchor, with P51 as the nearest type and a fit note: the statement protects the choice not to use AI, not cost or access.

units.why: "You are responsible for the accuracy and ethics of any artificial intelligence outputs" makes students answerable for output quality; P31 with the ownership aspect noted. Repeated in three samples; coded once.
units.anchor: You are responsible for the accuracy and ethics of any artificial intelligence outputs
units.fit_note: States responsibility for accuracy and ethics rather than an explicit duty to verify. Adds responsibility for ethics and does not say verify; closer to ownership (P29).

units.why: The mixed-use sample says 'For specific assignments (not all), AI may be used... only if explicitly permitted in the assignment instructions'; AI is allowed per assignment when stated, so P04 (per-assignment decision).
units.anchor: only if explicitly permitted in the assignment instructions
units.resolution_why: A coded may/permit on "AI may be used"; B coded may/restrict on "only if explicitly permitted in the assignment instructions". The mixed-use statement allows AI on specific assignments only when the instructions permit it, so the load-bearing words are B's condition and the unit_stance is restrict.

units.why: "to generate research questions or draft outlines" gives example permitted uses in the mixed-use policy, brainstorming and outlining; P15.
units.anchor: to generate research questions or draft outlines
units.fit_note: Examples only; permission applies only where assignment instructions allow.

units.why: "When permitted, you must cite your usage" requires a citation of AI use; P24.
units.anchor: When permitted, you must cite your usage

units.why: 'Unpermitted assignments (i.e., any assignment lacking explicit AI permissions) must be entirely your own work, without AI tools' defines the fallback: no explicit permission means no AI; P06.
units.anchor: any assignment lacking explicit AI permissions) must be entirely your own work
units.fit_note: Own-work requirement framed as a ban on AI tools for unpermitted assignments.
units.resolution_why: A split the sentence into two units (P06 fallback and P29 own work, must/prohibit); B coded one P06 unit. It is one rule: assignments without explicit AI permission are own work without AI tools. Kept one unit, P06, must-not (AI is barred) and dropped A's P29 duplicate, merging its fit note.

units.why: "If you are uncertain whether AI is allowed on a task, reach out for clarity" tells students to ask when unsure; P10.
units.anchor: If you are uncertain whether AI is allowed on a task, reach out for clarity
units.frag_start: If you are uncertain whether AI

units.why: "you will be expected to use AI in pursuit of the course learning objectives" is the optional addition for courses that expect AI use; P79 requires AI in coursework.
units.anchor: you will be expected to use AI in pursuit of the course learning objectives
units.frag_start: For one or more assignments in

units.why: 'the use of AI remains optional. If you would rather not use AI, that is perfectly acceptable' is the optional variant of required assignments; students may opt out, P51.
units.anchor: If you would rather not use AI, that is perfectly acceptable
units.frag_start: the use of AI remains optional.
units.fit_note: Protects the choice not to use AI on a required-AI assignment, not cost or access.
units.resolution_why: Found only by B: "If you would rather not use AI, that is perfectly acceptable" in the required-AI addition, a separate sentence from the instructor accommodation. A coded only the accommodation sentence. Real statement, kept.

units.why: "the use of AI remains optional" with "accommodations or alternative assignments" preserves choice for required-AI assignments; P51.
units.anchor: accommodations or alternative assignments can be made
units.frag_start: the use of AI remains optional
units.resolution_why: A coded phase course-start, B during-work. The accommodation is offered for the specific required-AI assignments in the course, so during-work. Actor stays instructor: it is the instructor who commits to "accommodations or alternative assignments".

units.why: "you are required to use AI in the ways detailed by the professor" is the alternative statement making AI use mandatory; P79.
units.anchor: you are required to use AI in the ways detailed by the professor

notes: The faculty-handbook academic integrity page has no AI text, so not collected. No school or computing-unit policy found (Mathematics and Computer Science searched). Repeated accuracy-and-ethics sentence coded once (B's two later repeats dropped). Coder A's separate P29 unit for the unpermitted-assignment sentence merged into the P06 unit.
